title: A sea turtle's flippers are built for distance
description: A sea turtle cannot pull its flippers into its shell, and it does not need to. Those long front flippers work like wings underwater, flying the turtle across whole oceans.

body.heading: Flying, not paddling
paragraphs: Most turtles paddle. Sea turtles fly: their long, flattened front flippers beat in a figure-of-eight like a bird's wings, pushing water down and back, while the smaller rear flippers steer like a rudder.
The trade-off is life on land. Flippers built for the open ocean are clumsy on sand, which is why a nesting female's slow haul up the beach looks like such hard work — it is.

body.heading: Built to travel
paragraphs: That flying stroke is efficient enough to cross oceans. Some sea turtles migrate thousands of kilometres between feeding grounds and the beaches where they nest, navigating by senses scientists are still working to fully explain.
Seven species of sea turtle exist today, and all are threatened or endangered — one more reason the long journeys those flippers make deserve our protection, not just our admiration.

takeaway: Sea turtles fly through water on wing-like front flippers — magnificent for crossing oceans, clumsy on the sand where they nest.
